children: Global investment banking firm JP Morgan has set an end-2027 base-case target of 29,000 for the Nifty 50, implying roughly 12% upside from current levels, with a bull-case projection of 31,000 and a bear-case floor of 22,000.

In its latest India Equity Strategy report, on Friday, November 27, analysts Rajiv Batra and Rushit Mehta highlight a structural shift powering this outlook: a broadening private capital expenditure (capex) upcycle that has moved well beyond a handful of mega-cap conglomerates.

After years of pre-pandemic stagnation and sharp COVID-19 contractions, spending across roughly 15,000 non-PSU, non-financial companies (both listed and unlisted) has compounded at 14% annually from financial year 2022-2026, which is double the pandemic low.

Unlisted companies, including telecom and retail arms of major conglomerates as well as Indian units of global tech and electronics giants, account for more than half of India’s private capex every year, meaning listed-market data alone understates the true scale of the recovery, JPMorgan wrote in its note.

Cash-flow disclosures from roughly 2,350 listed companies show capital spending surged 25% YoY in the first half of the current financial year, with more than half of listed firms increasing capex every year for the past five years, the note added further.
Midcaps, Smallcaps, and New-Age Sectors Lead the Charge

In FY26, small-cap listed companies increased capex by 18%, twice the pace of the largest corporates. Within each market-cap tier, the top 50 mid-cap and small-cap spenders boosted capital outlay by roughly 50% in the first half of the current financial year.

Sectors supported by government initiatives, including solar, electronics, power equipment, data centres, defence, and electric vehicles (EVs), expanded capex by an estimated 30% in FY26 (following 35% growth in FY25), more than double the rate of traditional industries.
However, JP Morgan flags several headwinds that could temper the rally or trigger its bear-case scenario:
Spending pullbacks by major energy, cement, and telecom companies.
Higher borrowing costs for smaller firms, elevated food inflation, and potential interest rate hikes at home or by the US Federal Reserve.
A potential slowdown in government spending in 2H FY27 to meet fiscal deficit targets, alongside broader global macro shocks.
The Nifty 50 index needs to close above the 25,800 mark on Friday to register its fifth straight weekly advance, which will make it the longest weekly winning streak in over two years for the index.

title: Nifty 50 seen hitting 29,000 by 2027-end as JP Morgan spots broad private capex boom
